facts.text: Mary Dyer was hanged in Boston for repeatedly defying a law banning Quakers from the Massachusetts Bay Colony.

Charles II and Louis XIV signed a secret treaty, requiring England to aid France in its war against the Dutch Republic and the future conversion of Charles to Catholicism, in return for Louis making large payments to Charles and promising to aid him if there was a rebellion in England.
French Revolutionary Wars: A British fleet captured six French ships of the line in a naval battle off Ushant that came to be known as the Glorious First of June.

image.caption: Date 1 June 1794 Location 400 nautical miles (740 km) west of Ushant , Atlantic Ocean [ a ] [ 1 ] 47°24′N 17°27′W ﻿ / ﻿ 47.400°N 17.450°W ﻿ / 47.400; -17.450 Result See Aftermath

facts.text: War of 1812: Mortally wounded, U.S. Navy captain James Lawrence ordered his crew "Don't give up the ship!" as USS Chesapeake was captured by HMS Shannon off the coast of Boston.
British explorer James Clark Ross led the first expedition to reach the north magnetic pole.
The first land battle of the American Civil War after Fort Sumter took place in the village of Fairfax, Virginia.
The Navajo and the U.S. government signed the Treaty of Bosque Redondo, which allowed those interned at Fort Sumner to return to their ancestral lands.
World War II: The crews of three Japanese submarines scuttled their vessels and committed suicide after entering Sydney Harbour and launching a failed attack.

Eight German Junkers Ju 88s shot down British Overseas Airways Corporation Flight 777 over the Bay of Biscay off the coast of Spain and France, killing actor Leslie Howard and several other notable passengers.
The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty was ratified, banning all American and Soviet land-based missiles with a range of 500 to 5,500 km (310 to 3,420 mi).
Cyclone Gonu develops from an area of convection in the Arabian Sea, later becoming the worst recorded natural disaster in Oman.
The river cruise ship Dongfang zhi Xing capsized in the Yangtze, resulting in 442 deaths in China's worst peacetime maritime disaster.
For the first time since its transition to democracy, the Congress of Deputies in Spain passed a motion of no confidence against the government.

links.title: 2018 vote of no confidence in the government of Mariano Rajoy

facts.text: Scanian War: The Swedish warship Kronan, one of the largest ships in the world at the time, sank at the Battle of Öland with the loss of around 800 men.
The Revolution of the Ganhadores, the first general strike in Brazil, began in Salvador, Bahia.
In an informal article in a medical journal, Henry Heimlich introduced the concept of abdominal thrusts, commonly known as the Heimlich maneuver, to treat victims of choking.
Group representation constituencies were introduced to the parliament of Singapore.
On landing at Little Rock National Airport in the U.S. state of Arkansas, American Airlines Flight 1420 overran the runway and crashed, resulting in 11 deaths.
Napoleonic Wars: A Franco-Spanish fleet recaptured the British-held Diamond Rock, an uninhabited island at the entrance to the bay leading to Fort-de-France, Martinique.
The wedding of Grover Cleveland and Frances Folsom took place in the White House, in the only time that a U.S. president has married in the building.

links.title: Wedding of Grover Cleveland and Frances Folsom

facts.text: The USSR and Yugoslavia sign the Belgrade declaration, legitimising different interpretations of Marxism in non-Soviet countries.

Benno Ohnesorg, a German university student, was killed in West Berlin while protesting against the visit of Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi of Iran; the anarchist militant 2 June Movement was later named after the incident.
After an emergency landing due to an in-flight fire, 23 passengers aboard Air Canada Flight 797 were killed when a flashover occurred as the aircraft's doors opened.
Bosnian War: U.S. Air Force captain Scott O'Grady was shot down while patrolling the NATO no-fly zone over Bosnia, but ejected safely and was rescued six days later.
A gunman carried out a shooting spree in Cumbria, England, killing 12 people and injuring 11 others before committing suicide.

The Indian state of Telangana was officially formed, with K. Chandrashekar Rao becoming its first chief minister after his party, the Telangana Rashtra Samithi, secured a majority in the legislative assembly election.
Henry Hacking killed the Aboriginal Australian resistance fighter Pemulwuy after Philip Gidley King ordered that he be brought in dead or alive.
First Red Scare: The anarchist followers of Luigi Galleani set off eight bombs in eight cities across the United States.
Queen Elizabeth II was crowned at Westminster Abbey in London.
Della Aleksander co-presented an episode of Open Door on transgender women's lives.
A collision between two passenger trains and a parked freight train near the city of Balasore, Odisha, in eastern India resulted in 296 deaths and more than 1,200 people injured.
Anglo-Spanish War: The English navy defeated a Spanish–Portuguese fleet off Sesimbra, Portugal, and captured a carrack.
Pope Alexander VII appointed François de Laval as the first apostolic vicar of New France.

Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo, a historic Catholic mission church in present-day Carmel-by-the-Sea, California, and the site of the first Christian confirmation in Alta California, was established.

links.title: Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo

facts.text: The last known pair of great auks, the only modern species in the genus Pinguinus of flightless birds, were killed on Eldey, Iceland.

image.caption: Specimen No. 8 and replica egg in the Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum , Glasgow

facts.text: The British merchant ship Virago sank off Alderney with the loss of 26 crew.
A socialist convention in Leeds, United Kingdom, called for an end to the First World War and the establishment of Workers' and Soldiers' Delegates across the country.

links.title: Council of Workers' and Soldiers' Delegates

facts.text: At his trial for the assassination of Talaat Pasha, viewed as the main orchestrator of the Armenian genocide, Soghomon Tehlirian was acquitted after arguing: "I have killed a man, but I am not a murderer."
Franz Rademacher, a Nazi official, proposed that the island of Madagascar be made available as a destination for the resettlement of the Jewish population of Europe.
Maurice Herzog and Louis Lachenal, members of the French Annapurna expedition, became the first climbers to reach the summit of a peak higher than 8,000 metres (26,247 ft) above sea level.
Buddhist crisis: South Vietnamese soldiers attacked Buddhist protesters in Huế with liquid chemicals from tear gas grenades, causing 67 people to be hospitalised.
American radical feminist Valerie Solanas shot and wounded visual artist Andy Warhol and two others at Warhol's New York City studio, The Factory.
At the Paris Air Show, a Tupolev Tu-144 broke up in mid-air, killing all six members of its crew and eight bystanders on the ground.
Having invaded Uganda and deposed President Idi Amin, Tanzanian forces secured Uganda's western border, ending a seven-month war.
Prime minister of Mongolia Luvsannamsrain Oyun-Erdene resigned after weeks of protests.
American Revolutionary War: Jack Jouett rode 40 miles (64 km) to warn Thomas Jefferson and the Virginia legislature of British cavalry who had been sent to capture them.
Liverpool F.C., one of England's most successful football clubs, was founded.
Half a year after abdicating the British throne, Edward, Duke of Windsor, married American socialite Wallis Simpson in a private ceremony in France.
During a SEATO exercise in the South China Sea, a collision between HMAS Melbourne and USS Frank E. Evans resulted in the latter vessel being cut in two and the deaths of 74 personnel.
A failed assassination attempt was made on Shlomo Argov, the Israeli ambassador to the United Kingdom, triggering an Israeli decision to invade Lebanon three days later.
The spire of Old St Paul's Cathedral in London was destroyed by fire.
Captain George Vancouver of the Royal Navy claimed the land around Puget Sound in the Pacific Northwest for Great Britain.
Emily Davison, an activist for women's suffrage in the United Kingdom, was fatally injured after being trampled by a horse owned by King George V at the Epsom Derby.

links.title: Women's suffrage in the United Kingdom

facts.text: World War I: Russian forces began their successful Brusilov offensive against the Central Powers.
The Kingdom of Hungary lost 72 percent of its territory and 64 percent of its population with the signing of the Treaty of Trianon in Paris.

Second World War: The remaining Allied forces protecting the Dunkirk evacuation surrendered, ending the Battle of Dunkirk; in response, British prime minister Winston Churchill gave a speech in which he declared " We shall fight on the beaches ".

links.title: We shall fight on the beaches

facts.text: World War II: The Battle of Midway, a major battle of the Pacific War, began with a massive Japanese offensive on American forces on Midway Atoll.
A chartered British Midland Airways aircraft crashed near Stockport, England, killing 72 of the 84 people on board.
Governor Jerry Brown signed the California Agricultural Labor Relations Act, one of the first laws in the United States guaranteeing collective bargaining rights to farmworkers.

links.title: California Agricultural Labor Relations Act of 1975

facts.text: The Humboldt Park riot began in Chicago, resulting in three deaths, three cars in the Humboldt Park lagoon, and increased tension between the Chicago Police Department and the Puerto Rican community.
Jerry Rawlings came to power in Ghana as chairman of the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council.
American intelligence analyst Jonathan Pollard pleaded guilty to charges of spying for Israel.
The People's Liberation Army suppressed the Tiananmen Square protests in Beijing, leaving hundreds of people dead and wounded.

links.title: People's Liberation Army at the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre

facts.text: Terry Nichols was sentenced to life in prison for his role in the Oklahoma City bombing.
In Granby, Colorado, U.S., Marvin Heemeyer went on a rampage with a modified bulldozer over a zoning dispute, destroying several buildings before committing suicide.
Élisabeth Thible became the first woman to fly in an untethered hot air balloon, covering a distance of 4 km (2.5 mi) and reaching an estimated altitude of 1,500 m (4,900 ft).
World War II: A United States Navy task group captured German submarine U-505.
Major League Baseball 's Cleveland Indians hosted Ten Cent Beer Night, but had to forfeit the game to the Texas Rangers due to rioting by drunken fans.
Following the death of Ruhollah Khomeini, the Assembly of Experts elected Ali Khamenei to be Supreme Leader of Iran.
The Daming Palace in Chang'an became the seat of government and the royal residence of the Tang dynasty during the reign of Emperor Gaozong.
Bolesław V, High Duke of Poland, granted city rights to Kraków modelled on the Magdeburg town charter.
Raymond Bertrand de Got was elected Pope Clement V, succeeding Benedict XI, who died the previous year.
The masque Tethys' Festival was performed at the Palace of Whitehall to celebrate the investiture of Henry Frederick as Prince of Wales.
The June Rebellion, an anti-monarchist uprising, broke out in Paris.
Vietnamese guerrilla leader Trương Định chose to fight on against European forces, defying Emperor Tự Đức and the Treaty of Saigon.
The Zungeni Mountain skirmish took place between British and Zulu forces during the second invasion of the Zulu Kingdom.
Second Sino-Japanese War: About 4,000 people died of asphyxiation in Chongqing when the tunnel in which they were hiding became blocked during a raid in the five-year bombing campaign.
British politician John Profumo admitted that he had lied to the House of Commons about his involvement in a sex scandal with Christine Keeler, and resigned from government.

links.title: House of Commons of the United Kingdom

facts.text: The arrest of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini for publicly denouncing Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi sparked protests in Iran.
Following Israel's initiation of Operation Focus with the goal to neutralise the Egyptian Air Force, Syrian Air Force, and the Royal Jordanian Air Force, the Six-Day War begins.
U.S. senator Robert F. Kennedy was fatally shot by Palestinian immigrant Sirhan Sirhan at the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles.

The Teton Dam in eastern Idaho, U.S., collapsed as its reservoir was being filled for the first time, resulting in the deaths of eleven people and 13,000 cattle, and causing up to $2 billion in damage.
The first clinical cases of AIDS were published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

links.title: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

facts.text: An anonymous demonstrator, later dubbed " Tank Man ", single-handedly stopped a column of Chinese tanks during the Tiananmen Square protests before being dragged aside.
Tropical Storm Allison, the costliest Atlantic tropical cyclone that was never a hurricane, made landfall in Texas, causing approximately $8.5 billion in damage.
A fire at a day-care center kills 49 children in Mexico
The Ancient Temples and Shrines Preservation Law was passed, instituting the protection of structures and artifacts in Japan designated National Treasures.
Antonio Luna, Commanding General of the Philippine Army, was assassinated in the midst of the Philippine–American War.
Anticipating a coup attempt, President Pascal Lissouba of the Republic of the Congo ordered the detention of his rival Denis Sassou Nguesso, initiating a second civil war.

links.title: Republic of the Congo Civil War (1997–1999)

facts.text: Noël Mamère, the mayor of Bègles, conducted a marriage ceremony for two men, even though same-sex marriage in France had not yet been legalised.
After almost two months of civil disobedience, at least 31 people were killed in clashes between the National Police and indigenous people in Bagua province, Peru.
War of the League of Cambrai: Milanese forces with Swiss mercenaries defeated the French in Novara, forcing them to withdraw from the Duchy of Milan and Italy.

links.title: War of the League of Cambrai

facts.text: Alexis St. Martin, a Canadian voyageur, was accidentally shot in the stomach; medical investigations of his injury led to a greater understanding of the processes of digestion.
American Civil War: The Union Army 's victory in the First Battle of Memphis virtually eradicated the Confederate naval presence on the Mississippi River.
The Shewan army defeated Gojjame forces at the Battle of Embabo, an event that contributed to the supremacy of Shewa within the Ethiopian Empire.
Governor Davis Hanson Waite ordered the Colorado state militia to protect and support miners engaged in a five-month strike in Cripple Creek.
Hughes Airwest Flight 706 collided with a US Marine Corps jet near Duarte, California, killing 50 people.
Vietnam War: Australian forces attacked a heavily fortified North Vietnamese base camp at the Battle of Long Khánh.
Falklands War: The Royal Navy destroyer HMS Cardiff engaged and destroyed a British Army helicopter in a friendly-fire incident.

links.title: 1982 British Army Gazelle friendly fire incident

facts.text: The remains of Josef Mengele, a Nazi physician notorious for performing human experiments on Auschwitz inmates, were exhumed in Embu das Artes, Brazil.
Syrian civil war: The Syrian Democratic Forces opened the Second Battle of Raqqa, the final phase of the Raqqa campaign, capturing the de facto capital of the Islamic State four months later.

image.caption: Date 6 June – 17 October 2017 (4 months, 1 week and 4 days) Location Raqqa , Raqqa Governorate , Syria 35°57′00″N 39°01′00″E ﻿ / ﻿ 35.9500°N 39.0167°E ﻿ / 35.9500; 39.0167 Result Decisive SDF and allies victory [ 9 ] 80% of the city is destroyed [ 10 ] Territorial changes The SDF captured 17th Division HQ on 8 June and completely encircled Raqqa on 24 June [ 11 ] [ 12 ] The SDF captured the city on 17 October [ 13 ]

facts.text: A man rammed a pickup truck into Muslim Pakistani Canadian pedestrians in Ontario, Canada, killing 4 members of the same family and injuring the family's nine year old son.
Shivaji, who led a resistance to free the Maratha from the Bijapur Sultanate and the Mughal Empire, was crowned the first chhatrapati of the Maratha Empire.
A plot by Muslim slaves in Malta to assassinate Manuel Pinto da Fonseca of the Knights Hospitaller was uncovered.

links.title: 1749 Muslim slave revolt plot in Malta

facts.text: War of 1812: The British ambushed an American encampment near present-day Stoney Creek, Ontario, capturing two senior officers.
The largest volcanic eruption of the 20th century began, forming the volcano Novarupta in the Alaska Peninsula.
World War II: Operation Overlord, the largest amphibious military operation in history, began with Allied troops landing on the beaches of Normandy in France.
Roman emperor Theodosius II married Aelia Eudocia, who later helped to protect Greek pagans and Jews from persecution.
An earthquake registering approximately 7.5 M w caused Port Royal, Jamaica, to sink below sea level and killed approximately 5,000 people.
Journalist Mariano Moreno published Argentina's first newspaper, the Gazeta de Buenos-Ayres.
The Reform Act, which is widely credited with launching modern democracy in the United Kingdom, received royal assent.
Homer Plessy, a mixed-race man from New Orleans, was arrested for refusing to leave his seat in the "whites-only" car of a train; he lost the resulting court case, Plessy v. Ferguson.
American temperance activist Carrie Nation entered a saloon in Kiowa, Kansas, and destroyed its stock of alcoholic beverages with rocks.

links.title: Temperance movement in the United States

facts.text: In Shostakovich v. Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corp., a New York trial court declined to issue a permanent injunction in favor of several Soviet composers against the distribution of The Iron Curtain, the first anti-Soviet Hollywood film of the Cold War era.

links.title: Shostakovich v. Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corp.

facts.text: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Griswold v. Connecticut that a Connecticut law prohibiting the use of contraceptives violated the "right to marital privacy".

links.title: Supreme Court of the United States

facts.text: The inaugural edition of the Cricket World Cup, the premier international championship of men's One Day International cricket, began in England.
The Israeli Air Force attacked a nuclear reactor under the assumption that it was about to start producing plutonium to further an Iraqi nuclear-weapons program.

links.title: Iraq and weapons of mass destruction

facts.text: White supremacists murdered James Byrd Jr., an African American, by chaining him behind a pickup truck and dragging him along an asphalt road in Jasper, Texas.
Pope John VIII officially recognised Croatia as an independent state, and Branimir as its duke.
The Petition of Right, a major English constitutional document that set out specific liberties of individuals, received royal assent from King Charles I.
First World War: The British Army detonated 19 ammonal mines under German lines, killing perhaps 10,000 in the deadliest non-nuclear man-made explosion in history during the Battle of Messines.

links.title: Mines in the Battle of Messines (1917)

facts.text: Anti-Jewish riots broke out in the French protectorate in Morocco, during which 44 people were killed and 150 injured.

links.title: 1948 anti-Jewish riots in Oujda and Jerada

facts.text: In their only UK concert, the rock supergroup Blind Faith, featuring Eric Clapton, Steve Winwood and Ginger Baker, debuted in London's Hyde Park in front of 100,000 fans.
Led by the inexperienced Gannys, Elagabalus 's legions defeated the forces of Roman emperor Macrinus at the Battle of Antioch.
American Revolutionary War: British forces defeated the Continental Army at the Battle of Trois-Rivières, the last battle of the American invasion of Quebec.
Laki, a volcanic fissure in Iceland, began an eight-month eruption, triggering a major famine and causing widespread fluoride poisoning.
American Civil War: The Confederate Army won a resounding victory at the Battle of Cross Keys, one of the two decisive battles in Jackson's Valley campaign.
Thomas Blamey became the only Australian to attain the rank of field marshal.
The Israeli Air Force attacked the U.S. Navy intelligence ship USS Liberty in international waters, killing 34 people and wounding 171 others.
Vietnam War: Associated Press photographer Nick Ut took a Pulitzer Prize–winning photograph of a naked nine-year-old Phan Thi Kim Phuc fleeing after being burned by napalm.

links.title: Pulitzer Prize for Breaking News Photography

facts.text: Falklands War: The Argentine Air Force attacked British transport ships while unloading supplies off Bluff Cove in the Falkland Islands, killing 56 British servicemen and wounding 150 others.
Falklands War: The Argentine Air Force attacked the neutral oil tanker Hercules while she was traversing the South Atlantic.
A major storm caused the bulk carrier Pasha Bulker to run aground in New South Wales, Australia.
A Japanese man drove a truck into a crowd of pedestrians in Akihabara, Tokyo, and proceeded to stab at least 12 people, killing 7 and wounding 10, before being apprehended.
Two American journalists, having been arrested for illegal entry into North Korea, were sentenced to twelve years hard labor before being pardoned two months later.

links.title: 2009 imprisonment of American journalists by North Korea

facts.text: In York, Upper Canada, members of the Family Compact destroyed William Lyon Mackenzie 's printing press in the Types Riot after Mackenzie accused them of corruption.
Margaret Bondfield became the first female member of the Cabinet of the United Kingdom when she was named Minister of Labour by Ramsay MacDonald.
World War II: The Allies commenced the Syria–Lebanon campaign against Vichy French possessions in the Levant.
An F5 tornado struck Flint and Beecher, Michigan, causing 116 fatalities, 844 injuries and $19 million in damage during a larger tornado outbreak sequence.
Abu Muslim initiated an open revolt against Umayyad rule, eventually leading to the establishment of the Abbasid Caliphate under the Black Standard.
Parisian printer Simon de Colines was fined for printing biblical commentary by Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples without obtaining prior approval from theologians.
The first company of Mormon handcart pioneers left Iowa City for Salt Lake City, Utah.
American Civil War: Confederate General Stonewall Jackson concluded his successful Shenandoah Valley campaign with a victory in the Battle of Port Republic.
American Civil War: Union and Confederate forces fought the Battle of Brandy Station, the largest cavalry engagement to take place on American soil.
Unhappy with U.S. president Woodrow Wilson 's handling of the RMS Lusitania sinking, William Jennings Bryan resigned as Secretary of State.

During hearings investigating conflicting accusations between the United States Army and Senator Joseph McCarthy, Army lawyer Joseph N. Welch asked McCarthy: " At long last, have you left no sense of decency? "
Fighting began between the Viet Cong and the Army of the Republic of Vietnam in the Battle of Đồng Xoài, one of the largest battles in the Vietnam War.

links.title: Army of the Republic of Vietnam

facts.text: The racehorse Secretariat, of Meadow Stables, won the Belmont Stakes by 31 lengths, achieving the first American Triple Crown victory in a quarter of a century.

links.title: Triple Crown of Thoroughbred Racing (United States)

facts.text: Lebanon War: The Israeli Air Force carried out Operation Mole Cricket 19, successfully suppressing Syrian air defenses in the Beqaa Valley, Lebanon.
A child suicide bomber attacked a wedding in Nadahan, Afghanistan, killing at least 40 people and injuring at least 70 others.
Dominican-American retired baseball player David Ortiz was shot and severely wounded while at a bar in Santo Domingo.
The first Book of Common Prayer was legally mandated by Parliament, introducing a fully vernacular Protestant liturgy to the Church of England.
In an act of defiance against the Navigation Acts, American colonists led by Abraham Whipple attacked and burned the British schooner Gaspee.
Australian aviator Charles Kingsford Smith and his crew landed the Southern Cross in Brisbane, completing the first transpacific flight.
Yugoslav Wars: The Kumanovo Agreement was signed, bringing an end to the Kosovo War the next day.
Tatwine was consecrated as Archbishop of Canterbury
Third Crusade: Frederick Barbarossa, Holy Roman Emperor, drowned in the Saleph River in Anatolia.
Byzantine–Ottoman wars: The heavily armed Byzantine army was defeated by Ottoman forces at the Battle of Pelekanon.
Bridget Bishop became the first person to be executed for witchcraft in the Salem witch trials in colonial Massachusetts.
King Rama I moved into the Grand Palace in Bangkok, which has remained the royal residence of Siam and Thailand since then.
At least 28 unarmed Indigenous Australians were massacred at Myall Creek, New South Wales.
The League of Prizren was officially founded to "struggle in arms to defend the wholeness of the territories of Albania".
Mount Tarawera, a volcano in New Zealand's North Island, erupted, killing around 120 people and creating the Waimangu Volcanic Rift Valley.
During a labor strike in Ipswich, Massachusetts, police opened fire into a crowd of strikers, killing one and injuring several others.
Hussein bin Ali, King of Hejaz, orchestrated a revolt against the Ottoman Empire with the aim of creating a single unified and independent Arab state.

links.title: Hussein bin Ali, King of Hejaz

facts.text: World War I: Italian torpedo boats sank the Austro-Hungarian dreadnought SMS Szent István off the Dalmatian coast, killing 89 of the crew.
The United Church of Canada, the country's largest Protestant denomination, held its inaugural service at the Mutual Street Arena in Toronto.
American physician Bob Smith had his last alcoholic drink, marking the traditional founding date of Alcoholics Anonymous.
The Royal New Zealand Navy adopted a unique white ensign, to distinguish its vessels from those of the Royal Navy.
Eleven-year-old Jaycee Dugard was kidnapped in South Lake Tahoe, California; she remained a captive until 2009.
War in Afghanistan: A U.S. airstrike resulted in the reported deaths of eleven paramilitary members of the Pakistani Frontier Corps and eight Taliban fighters in Pakistan's tribal areas.
Sudan Airways Flight 109 crashed on landing at Khartoum International Airport, killing 30 of the 214 occupants on board.
A plane crash in Malawi, kills nine people, including Vice President Saulos Chilima.
Thirty Years' War: France and the Dutch Republic concluded the Treaty of Compiègne, a mutual defence alliance.
Ten days after being formed by an earthquake, a landslide dam on the Dadu River in China was destroyed by an aftershock, causing a flood that killed an estimated 100,000 people.
American Civil War: The Confederate Army only suffered eight casualties in its victory at the Battle of Big Bethel in York County, Virginia.
Led by John Diefenbaker, the Progressive Conservative Party won a plurality of House of Commons seats in the Canadian federal election.
Mass protests demanding direct presidential elections broke out across South Korea.
Arab–Byzantine wars: The Abbasid army departed Raqqa in northern Syria to begin an invasion of Byzantine -controlled Asia Minor.
Inspecting a new prison without being escorted by his bodyguard, the megas doux Alexios Apokaukos, chief minister of the Byzantine Empire, was lynched by the prisoners.
Catherine of Aragon married King Henry VIII of England, becoming the first of his six wives.
The Battle of Machias, the first naval engagement of the American Revolutionary War, commenced in and around the port of Machias in what is now eastern Maine.
Tensions between Yankees and Irish Americans in Boston, Massachusetts, erupted in the Broad Street Riot.
Prince Afonso died at the age of two, leaving his father Pedro II, the last emperor of Brazil, without a male heir.
Alexander was crowned King of Greece, succeeding his father Constantine I, who had abdicated.

During their national convention in Chicago, Republican Party leaders gathered in negotiations at The Blackstone Hotel to select their presidential candidate, leading to the phrase " smoke-filled room ".
Kitosh, an African labourer, died after having been flogged by his British employer, in a case that eventually led to reform of the legal system of the Kenya Colony.
American criminals Clarence Anglin, John Anglin and Frank Morris escaped from Alcatraz Island, one of the United States' most famous prisons.
Vietnamese monk Thích Quảng Đức burned himself to death in Saigon to protest the persecution of Buddhists by Catholic South Vietnamese President Ngo Dinh Diem 's administration.
Timothy McVeigh, detonator of a truck bomb in front of the Oklahoma federal building, was executed by lethal injection for using a weapon of mass destruction, among other charges.
Robert Edward Dyer was sentenced to 16 years' imprisonment for conducting a six-month-long letter-bomb campaign against the British supermarket chain Tesco.
Mudslides caused by heavy monsoon rainfall and exacerbated by hill cutting killed at least 128 people in Chittagong, Bangladesh.
Canadian prime minister Stephen Harper apologised to the First Nations for past governments' policies of forced assimilation.
The semi-professional English football club Gedling Town F.C. withdrew from league football, shortly before its dissolution.
Two earthquakes struck northern Afghanistan, triggering a massive landslide that buried a village and killed 75 people.
Philip II of Spain recognized the sovereign rights of the principalía, local Philippine nobles and chieftains who had converted to Catholicism.
J. S. Bach led his cantata O Ewigkeit, du Donnerwort, BWV 20, in Leipzig on the first Sunday after Trinity, beginning his chorale cantata cycle.

links.title: List of church cantatas by liturgical occasion

facts.text: Around 2,000 members of European society attended a ball at Kenwood House, England, in one of the last major social events before the outbreak of the First World War.
The University of Alabama was desegregated as Governor George Wallace stepped aside after defiantly blocking the entrance to an auditorium.

links.title: Racial segregation in the United States

facts.text: Thomas Gage, the governor of the Province of Massachusetts Bay, offered a general pardon to colonists who remained loyal to Britain.
Following the successful French invasion of Malta, the Knights Hospitaller surrendered Malta to Napoleon, initiating two years of occupation.
Union general Ulysses S. Grant pulled his troops out of the Battle of Cold Harbor in Hanover County, Virginia, ending one of the bloodiest, most lopsided battles in the American Civil War.
As part of the Ottoman Empire 's policies of ethnic cleansing, Turkish irregulars began a six-day massacre in the predominantly Greek town of Phocaea.
Soviet politician Vladimir Antonov-Ovseenko authorised the use of chemical weapons against a peasant rebellion in the Tambov Governorate.
On her thirteenth birthday, Anne Frank began keeping a diary during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands in World War II.

image.caption: Born Annelies Marie Frank ( 1929-06-12 ) 12 June 1929 Frankfurt , Germany

links.title: The Diary of a Young Girl

facts.text: Dominic Savio, who was 14 years old at his death in 1857, was canonized by Pope Pius XII, making him one of the youngest non- martyred saints in the Catholic Church.
The premiere was held in New York of the historical drama film Cleopatra, the most expensive film made to that point.
The U.S. Supreme Court struck down laws restricting interracial marriage in the landmark civil rights case Loving v. Virginia.

links.title: Supreme Court of the United States
Anti-miscegenation laws in the United States

facts.text: American serial killer David Berkowitz, popularly known as the "Son of Sam", was sentenced to 25-years-to-life in prison for each of six killings.
Cold War: During a speech at the Brandenburg Gate by the Berlin Wall, US president Ronald Reagan challenged Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev to " tear down this wall! " (speech featured).
More than 150 Sri Lankan Tamil civilians were massacred by members of the military in the village of Kokkadichcholai.
The Boeing 777, the world's largest twinjet, made its maiden flight.
Sixteen-year-old Abby Sunderland was rescued after her boat was dismasted in the Indian Ocean while trying to become the youngest sailor around the world.
An Islamic terrorist killed 49 people in a mass shooting at the gay nightclub Pulse in Orlando, Florida.
The Disputation of Paris, in which four rabbis defended the Talmud against Nicholas Donin 's accusations of blasphemy, began in the court of King Louis IX.
The Fifth Virginia Convention adopted a declaration of rights, an influential document that proclaimed the inherent rights of men.
Raiders of the Lost Ark, the first film to star Harrison Ford as Indiana Jones, was released.
In the aftermath of the bombing of Yugoslavia and the Kosovo War, the NATO -led Kosovo Force entered Kosovo with a mandate of establishing a secure environment in the territory.
Air India Flight 171 crashes shortly after take-off in Ahmedabad, India, killing 260 people.
Henry Grace à Dieu, the largest warship ever built at the time, was launched from Woolwich Dockyard, England.
Lewis and Clark Expedition: Meriwether Lewis became the first white American to sight the Great Falls of the Missouri River.
The American League of Colored Laborers, one of the first labor unions for African Americans, was established in New York City.
World War I: The Battle of Mont Sorrel in the Ypres Salient came to an end as a Canadian assault led German forces to withdraw to their original lines.
In one of the biggest upsets in championship boxing, the underdog James J. Braddock defeated Max Baer to become the heavyweight champion of the world.

links.title: List of world heavyweight boxing champions

facts.text: Second World War: At the Battle of Villers-Bocage, German tank commander Michael Wittmann destroyed around 30 Allied vehicles in less than 15 minutes.
" The Long and Winding Road " became the Beatles ' twentieth and final number-one single on the Billboard Hot 100 chart.

The New York Times published the first excerpts from the Pentagon Papers, a 7,000-page classified Department of Defense history of the United States' political and military involvement in the Vietnam War.
English teenager Marcus Sarjeant fired six blanks at Queen Elizabeth II as she rode down The Mall to the Trooping the Colour ceremony.
Pioneer 10 passed the orbit of Neptune, becoming the first man-made object to leave the proximity of the major planets of the Solar System.
Insurgents carried out a second bombing at the al-Askari Mosque, one of the holiest sites in Shia Islam.
A 6.0 M w earthquake caused up to NZ$6 billion of additional damage to Christchurch, New Zealand, which was still recovering from an earthquake four months earlier.
Martin Luther married Katharina von Bora, beginning the practice of clerical marriage in Protestantism.

The Jeannette expedition to reach the North Pole from the Pacific Ocean via the Bering Strait came to an end when the USS Jeannette, after having been trapped in ice for almost two years, was crushed and sank.
Soviet aircraft shot down a Swedish military plane carrying out signals-intelligence gathering operations, followed three days later by the shootdown of a second plane searching for the first one.
Preston Smith, Governor of Texas, signed a law converting a research arm of Texas Instruments into the University of Texas at Dallas.
Some of the closest advisors and collaborators of Czech prime minister Petr Nečas were arrested for corruption.
Franco-Spanish War: French and Spanish fleets fought the inconclusive Battle of Orbetello, with sailing vessels of both sides having to be towed into action by galleys due to light winds.
The Second Continental Congress adopted the stars and stripes design for the flag of the United States.
War of the Second Coalition: In the Battle of Marengo, Napoleonic forces secured victory over the Habsburgs when defeat had appeared inevitable until the arrival of French troops led by Louis Desaix.

In a paper presented to the Royal Astronomical Society, English mathematician Charles Babbage proposed a difference engine, an automatic, mechanical calculator designed to tabulate polynomial functions.
Settlers in Sonoma began rebelling against Mexico, later proclaiming the California Republic and raising a homemade flag with a bear and a star.
The second of the German Naval Laws was passed, authorising the doubling in size of the Imperial German Navy.
The landmark Australian Eastern Mission concluded after a three-month diplomatic tour of East and South-East Asia.
The Soviet Union issued an ultimatum to Lithuania demanding that the Red Army be allowed to enter the country and form a pro-Soviet government.
Second World War: Four days after the French government fled Paris, German forces occupied the French capital, a major accomplishment in the Fall Rot operation.
Second World War: The British Army abandoned its attempt to capture the German-occupied city of Caen.
The Vatican formally abolished its 427-year-old list of prohibited books.
Emerson, Lake & Palmer released the progressive rock album Tarkus.
Falklands War: British prime minister Margaret Thatcher announced that white flags were flying over Port Stanley, in advance of the formal surrender of Argentine forces.

links.title: Argentine surrender in the Falklands War

facts.text: Swedish woman Helena Andersson disappeared in Mariestad, one suspect were ”the man with the pilot glasses".
After an 81-day standoff sparked by their refusal to be evicted from their foreclosed property in Jordan, Montana, the Christian Patriot group Montana Freemen surrendered to the FBI.
A fire severely damaged Grenfell Tower in North Kensington, London, killing 72 people.

links.title: Aftermath of the Grenfell Tower fire

facts.text: During the Peasants' Revolt in England, rebels stormed the Tower of London, killing Simon Sudbury, Lord Chancellor, and Robert Hales, Lord High Treasurer.

image.caption: Date 30 May – November 1381 Location England Result Sacking of Tower of London and mass execution of royal officials Charters granted to rebel towns Eventual suppression of revolt and execution of rebel leaders

facts.text: First English Civil War: Prince Maurice abandoned his siege of Lyme Regis in Dorset after learning of the approach of a Parliamentarian relief force.
War in Donbas: An Ilyushin Il-76 transport aircraft of the Ukrainian Air Force was shot down by forces of the self-proclaimed Luhansk People's Republic, killing all 49 people on board.

links.title: 2014 Ukrainian Air Force Ilyushin Il-76 shootdown

facts.text: Pope Leo X issued the papal bull Exsurge Domine, censuring 41 propositions from Martin Luther 's Ninety-five Theses and subsequent writings, and threatening him with excommunication unless he recanted.
The shooting of a pig in the San Juan Islands led to the so-called Pig War over the border between the United States and British North America.
An earthquake registering 8.5 M w and subsequent tsunami struck Japan, killing at least 22,000 people and destroying about 9,000 homes.
Three African-American circus workers were lynched by a mob in Duluth, Minnesota, a crime that shocked the country for having taken place in the Northern United States.
Bessie Coleman became the first Black person to earn an international pilot's license from the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale.
King Hussein of Jordan married American Lisa Halaby, who became known as Queen Noor of Jordan.
The eruption of Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines deposited large amounts of particulate matter into the atmosphere, enough to lower global temperatures by about 0.5 °C (0.9 °F).
Western Greece was struck by an earthquake registering 6.4–6.5 M w that killed 26 people.
Leaders of China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan formed the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation.

US president George W. Bush designated 140,000 square miles (360,000 km 2 ) around the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands as the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, now one of the world's largest protected areas.
American acrobat Nik Wallenda became the first person to walk a tightrope stretched directly over Niagara Falls.
King John of England and a group of rebel barons agreed on the text of Magna Carta, an influential charter of rights.
War of the Second Coalition: The signing of the Convention of Alessandria brought temporary peace between France and Austria.
Eadweard Muybridge took a series of photographs to prove that all four feet of a horse leave the ground when it gallops, which became the basis of motion pictures.
World War II: The United States Army Air Forces began the first air raid of its strategic bombing campaign against the Japanese archipelago, although little damage was caused.
The Troubles: The Provisional Irish Republican Army detonated a truck bomb in the commercial centre of Manchester, England, injuring more than 200 people and causing widespread damage to buildings.
Ming forces conquered Đại Ngu in modern-day northern Vietnam, capturing Hồ dynasty emperor Hồ Quý Ly and bringing the country under Chinese rule.
The Plymouth Company granted a land patent to Thomas Purchase, who became the first permanent European settler of Pejepscot, Maine.
After a two-week siege, the French commander of Fort Beauséjour in present-day New Brunswick, Canada, surrendered to British forces, marking the end of Father Le Loutre's War.
In the Victoria Hall disaster, 183 children were crushed to death when they ran down the stairs to collect gifts after a variety show in Sunderland, England.
The technology company IBM was founded as the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company in Endicott, New York.
Psycho, a psychological horror film directed by Alfred Hitchcock and based on a novel of the same name by Robert Bloch, premiered.
Aboard Vostok 6, Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space.
English musician David Bowie released his breakthrough album, The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars.

links.title: The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars

facts.text: Liu Yang, a member of the Shenzhou 9 crew, became the first Chinese woman in space.
Jo Cox, a British Member of Parliament, was murdered in her constituency.
The final king of the Sasanian Empire of Iran, Yazdegerd III, ascended the throne at the age of eight.
A strong earthquake in the Kutch district of Gujarat, India, caused a local zone of uplift that dammed the Nara River, which was later named the Allah Bund ('Dam of God').
Irish author James Joyce began a relationship with Nora Barnacle, and subsequently used the date to set the actions for his 1922 novel Ulysses, commemorated as Bloomsday.
A Junkers Ju 52 aircraft of Norwegian Air Lines crashed into a mountainside near Hyllestad, Norway, killing all seven people on board.
The English rock band Radiohead released their landmark third album OK Computer in the United Kingdom.
Pope Martin I was arrested in the Lateran Palace, Rome, and taken to Constantinople.
The kingdoms of Denmark, Sweden, and Norway formed the Kalmar Union, a personal union under Eric of Pomerania.
Hungarian–Ottoman Wars: Wallachian forces led by Vlad Dracula attacked an Ottoman camp at night in an unsuccessful attempt to assassinate Sultan Mehmed II.
American Revolutionary War: British forces took Bunker Hill outside of Boston, Massachusetts.
French Revolutionary Wars: Off the coast of Brittany, a Royal Navy squadron commanded by William Cornwallis fended off a numerically superior French Navy fleet.

image.caption: Date 16–17 June 1795 Location Off Brittany , Atlantic Ocean Result British victory

facts.text: American Civil War: The Battle of Vienna, Virginia, took place, which involved one of the world's first military movements of troops by train.
Boxer Rebellion: Allied naval forces captured the Taku Forts from Qing China after a brief but bloody battle.
In Detroit, autoworkers for car manufacturer Studebaker went on strike in the American auto industry's first major strike action.
Second World War: RMS Lancastria was sunk by German aircraft near Saint-Nazaire, France, causing thousands of fatalities in Britain's worst maritime disaster.
Riots broke out in Saigon one day after the signing of the Joint Communiqué, an attempt to resolve the Buddhist crisis in South Vietnam.
Following a petition, the liberal progressive Czech Pirate Party was officially registered as a political party.
A white supremacist committed a mass shooting at the Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston, South Carolina, killing nine people during a prayer service.
Wildfires erupted across central Portugal, eventually causing the deaths of 66 people.
Explorer Francis Drake landed in a region of present-day California, naming it New Albion and claiming it for England.
Mumtaz Mahal, wife of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, died in childbirth; Jahan spent the next seventeen years constructing her mausoleum, the Taj Mahal.

links.title: List of emperors of the Mughal Empire
Origins and architecture of the Taj Mahal

facts.text: Hundreds of Canadian soldiers rioted in Epsom, England, leading to the death of a British police officer.
Guatemalan Revolution: The Guatemalan Congress passed Decree 900, redistributing unused land greater than 224 acres (0.91 km 2 ) in area to local peasants.

links.title: Congress of the Republic of Guatemala

facts.text: Sui–Tang transition: Chinese governor Li Yuan declared himself emperor, establishing the Tang dynasty.
Rus' forces sailed into the Bosporus in a fleet of about 200 vessels and started pillaging the suburbs of Constantinople.
Third Silesian War: The Austrian victory at the Battle of Kolín forced Prussian leader Frederick the Great to give up the Siege of Prague and retreat to Saxony.
War of the Seventh Coalition: Napoleon fought and lost his final battle, the Battle of Waterloo (depicted), in present-day Belgium.
Charles Darwin received a manuscript by fellow naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace on natural selection, which encouraged him to publish his own theory of evolution.

links.title: On the Tendency of Species to form Varieties; and on the Perpetuation of Varieties and Species by Natural Means of Selection

facts.text: World War II: Charles de Gaulle gave his Appeal of 18 June speech, often considered to be the origin of the French Resistance.
A Douglas C-124 Globemaster II aircraft crashed just after takeoff from Tachikawa, Japan, killing all 129 people on board.
Carlos Castillo Armas led a CIA -sponsored invasion force across the Guatemalan border, beginning the 1954 Guatemalan coup d'état.

British European Airways Flight 548 crashed near Staines-upon-Thames less than three minutes after departing from Heathrow Airport in London, killing all 118 people aboard in the worst air accident in the UK.
Iranian teenager Mona Mahmudnizhad and nine other women were hanged in Shiraz because of their membership in the Baháʼí Faith.
Aboard Space Shuttle Challenger, astronaut Sally Ride became the first American woman and third one overall in space.
Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud was appointed the crown prince of Saudi Arabia.
The Cadaver Tomb of René of Chalon in Bar-le-Duc, France, was designated a monument historique.

links.title: Cadaver Tomb of René of Chalon

facts.text: English composer Benjamin Britten 's one-act opera Noye's Fludde was premiered at the Aldeburgh Festival.
American musician Jimi Hendrix burned his guitar on stage at the end of a performance at the Monterey International Pop Festival in California.
The Lockheed F-117 Nighthawk, the first operational aircraft to be designed around stealth technology, made its maiden flight.
The Troubles: Ulster Volunteer Force members attacked a crowded bar in Loughinisland, Northern Ireland, with assault rifles, killing six people.
An earthquake on the Tibetan Plateau led to the deaths of more than 73,000 people.
The first officially recorded baseball game in U.S. history using modern rules was played in Hoboken, New Jersey, with the "New York Nine" defeating the New York Knickerbockers 23–1.
Second French intervention in Mexico: Emperor Maximilian I of Mexico was executed by firing squad in Querétaro City.
Americans Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were executed as spies for passing nuclear weapons secrets to the Soviet Union.

image.caption: Born Julius Rosenberg ( 1918-05-12 ) May 12, 1918 New York City , U.S. Ethel Greenglass ( 1915-09-28 ) September 28, 1915 New York City, U.S.

facts.text: Nguyễn Cao Kỳ, the commander of the South Vietnam Air Force, was appointed prime minister at the head of a military regime.
The international Patent Cooperation Treaty was signed, providing a unified procedure for filing patent applications to protect inventions in each of its contracting states.
The Basque separatist group ETA detonated a car bomb at a Hipercor shopping centre in Barcelona, killing 21 people and injuring 45 others.
Only six race cars competed in the United States Grand Prix at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway in Indianapolis, Indiana, after all the Michelin -shod entrants were withdrawn due to safety concerns.
Mass rioting broke out in Shishou, China, over the dubious circumstances surrounding the death of a local chef.
The royal wedding of Victoria, Crown Princess of Sweden, and Daniel Westling took place in Stockholm Cathedral.

links.title: Wedding of Victoria, Crown Princess of Sweden, and Daniel Westling

facts.text: Facing allegations of sexual assault in Sweden, Julian Assange, the founder of WikiLeaks, requested asylum at the Ecuadorian embassy in London.

image.caption: Born Julian Paul Hawkins ( 1971-07-03 ) 3 July 1971 (age 54) Townsville , Queensland , Australia

facts.text: The proprietors of King's Chapel, Boston, voted to adopt James Freeman 's Book of Common Prayer, thus establishing the first Unitarian church in the Americas.
The Maryland province of the Jesuits contracted to sell 272 slaves to buyers in Louisiana in one of the largest slave sales in American history.
American baseball player Lou Gehrig was diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, now commonly known in the United States as "Lou Gehrig's disease".
War in Afghanistan: British forces began Operation Panther's Claw, in which more than 350 troops made an aerial assault on Taliban positions in southern Afghanistan.
The Congress of the Confederation adopted the Great Seal of the United States, used to authenticate documents issued by the U.S. federal government.

links.title: Great Seal of the United States
Federal government of the United States

facts.text: Boxer Rebellion: The Imperial Chinese Army began a 55-day siege of the Legation Quarter in Peking.
Workers at the Buckingham and Carnatic Mills in Madras, India, began a four-month strike.
Approximately 250,000 spectators attended the opening procession of the 28th International Eucharistic Congress in Chicago, United States.
World War II: The Royal Air Force began Operation Bellicose, a four-day shuttle-bombing mission that included raids on Germany and Italy and a refuelling and rearming stop in Algeria.
A Mafia hitman murdered gangster Bugsy Siegel, one of the driving forces in the development of the Las Vegas Strip, in Beverly Hills, California.
The Mali Federation gained independence from France, but dissolved into Mali and Senegal two months later.
Steven Spielberg 's film Jaws was released; it became a summer blockbuster and the first film to earn $100 million in U.S. theatrical rentals.
A bomb explosion in the Imam Reza shrine in Mashhad, Iran, left at least 25 dead and more than 70 injured.

Iranian student Neda Agha-Soltan was shot dead in Tehran during the presidential election protests; footage of her death was widely distributed over the Internet, making it "probably the most widely witnessed death in human history".
Iranian aircraft shot down an American drone over the Strait of Hormuz amid heightened tensions between the two countries.
Queen Victoria acceded to the British throne, beginning a 63-year reign.
British Army officer Thomas Stanton Lambert was assassinated by the Irish Republican Army near Moydrum, Ireland.
The extratropical remnants of an Atlantic hurricane reached the Gulf of St. Lawrence in Canada, causing 22 fishing boats to capsize and killing 35 people.
Bill Stewart, an American journalist, was executed by Nicaraguan Guardia forces.

The International Conference on the Holocaust and Genocide, the first major conference in genocide studies, opened despite Turkish attempts to cancel it due to the inclusion of presentations on the Armenian genocide.

links.title: International Conference on the Holocaust and Genocide

facts.text: William Clito defeated Thierry of Alsace in a battle over the succession to the title of Count of Flanders.
War of the League of Cognac: The French army under Francis de Bourbon was destroyed in Lombardy, Italy, by the Spanish army.

links.title: War of the League of Cognac
Francis de Bourbon, Count of St. Pol

facts.text: French Wars of Religion: Catholic forces defeated an armed group of Huguenots attempting to capture Besançon, from which they had previously been expelled.
New Hampshire ratified the U.S. Constitution and was admitted as the ninth U.S. state.
Greek War of Independence: A combined Egyptian and Ottoman army began an invasion of the Mani Peninsula, but were initially held off by the Maniots at the fortifications of Vergas.
New Zealand Wars: A British victory against the Māori King Movement brought the Tauranga campaign to an end.
Rudyard Kipling 's poem Mandalay was published.
Admiral Ludwig von Reuter scuttled the German High Seas Fleet in Scapa Flow to prevent the ships from being seized and divided amongst the Allied Powers.

links.title: Scuttling of the German fleet at Scapa Flow

facts.text: Irish War of Independence: Most of the village of Knockcroghery in County Roscommon was burned by British forces.
World War II: The main offensive of the unsuccessful Italian invasion of France began.
Ellen Fairclough became the first woman to be appointed to the cabinet of Canada.
The U.S. Supreme Court delivered its decision in the landmark case Miller v. California, establishing the Miller test for determining what is obscene material.

links.title: Supreme Court of the United States
List of landmark court decisions in the United States

facts.text: President Bill Clinton awarded the Medal of Honor to 22 Asian Americans, mostly from the 442nd Regimental Combat Team, for actions during World War II.

links.title: List of Asian Pacific American Medal of Honor recipients

facts.text: In the Wallachian Revolution, Ion Heliade Rădulescu and Christian Tell proclaimed a new republican government in present-day Romania.
In a bloodless event during the Spanish–American War, the United States captured Guam from Spain.
During a general strike in Winnipeg, Canada, members of the Royal North-West Mounted Police attacked a crowd of strikers, armed with clubs and revolvers.
The Manchester Baby, the world's first stored-program computer, ran its first program.

image.caption: Also known as Small-Scale Experimental Machine

facts.text: The British warship HMS Leopard pursued and attacked the American frigate USS Chesapeake in the belief that the crew of the latter included deserters from the Royal Navy.

image.caption: Date June 22, 1807 Location off Norfolk, Virginia Result British victory

facts.text: France declared war on Russia, starting Napoleon's invasion two days later.

links.title: 1812 French declaration of war on Russia

facts.text: War of 1812: After learning of a forthcoming American attack, Laura Secord walked 20 mi (32 km) from Queenston, Upper Canada, to warn British lieutenant James FitzGibbon (depicted).
Irish Republican Army gunmen assassinated British member of parliament Field Marshal Sir Henry Wilson.
World War II: German minister of foreign affairs Joachim von Ribbentrop presented a declaration of war to the Soviet ambassador Vladimir Dekanozov in Berlin.

links.title: German declaration of war on the Soviet Union

facts.text: Vietnamese Buddhist activist leader Thích Trí Quang was arrested as the military junta of Nguyễn Cao Kỳ crushed the Buddhist Uprising.
Two Metro trains collided in Washington, D.C., killing nine people and injuring eighty others.
An earthquake registering 6.2 M w caused the deaths of at least 1,000 people in Afghanistan and Pakistan.
Habsburg troops defeated a larger Ottoman force at the Battle of Sisak in the Kingdom of Croatia, triggering the Long Turkish War.
King George V and Queen Mary were crowned at Westminster Abbey in London.

image.caption: King of the United Kingdom and the British Dominions Emperor of India

links.title: Coronation of George V and Mary

facts.text: World War II: As Axis troops began their invasion of the Soviet Union, the Lithuanian Activist Front started an uprising to liberate Lithuania from Soviet occupation.

links.title: Soviet occupation of the Baltic states (1940)

facts.text: Former British Liberal Party leader Jeremy Thorpe was acquitted of conspiracy to murder Norman Scott, who had accused Thorpe of having a relationship with him.
A magnitude-6.5 earthquake struck northwestern Iran, killing at least 230 people and injuring 1,300 others; the official response, perceived to be slow, later caused widespread public anger.
Reconquista: Troops of the Emirate of Granada defeated those of the Kingdom of Castile and the Kingdom of León in the Battle of Moclín.

Anglo-Spanish War: During the Action of Faial, an English attempt to capture a Portuguese carrack, reputedly one of the richest ever to set sail from the Indies, caused it to explode with all the treasure lost.
War of the First Coalition: Napoleon signed the Armistice of Bologna, agreeing a ceasefire between France and the Papal States.
The College Board administered the first SAT, a major standardized test for university and college admissions in the United States.
The Holocaust: After a closely supervised visit to Theresienstadt Ghetto in German-occupied Czechoslovakia, Red Cross official Maurice Rossel reported that conditions there were "almost normal".

links.title: Theresienstadt Ghetto and the Red Cross
International Committee of the Red Cross

facts.text: Canada's largest recorded onshore earthquake struck Vancouver Island, British Columbia.
In a nationwide referendum, Gamal Abdel Nasser was elected President of Egypt, a post he held until his death in 1970.
President Richard Nixon signed Title IX into law as part of the Education Amendments, prohibiting gender discrimination in any educational program receiving U.S. federal funds.

image.caption: Long title An Act to amend the Higher Education Act of 1965, the Vocational Education Act of 1963, the General Education Provisions Act (creating a National Foundation for Postsecondary Education and a National Institute of Education), the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965, Public Law 874, Eighty-first Congress, and related Acts, and for other purposes.

links.title: Administration of federal assistance in the United States

facts.text: The Los Angeles Dodgers started Steve Garvey, Davey Lopes, Ron Cey, and Bill Russell in the infield, beginning a record eight-year run in Major League Baseball for four people designated as starters for those positions.

links.title: Dodger infield of Garvey, Lopes, Cey and Russell

facts.text: Chinese American Vincent Chin died after being beaten into a coma in Highland Park, Michigan, U.S., by two automotive workers who were angry about the success of Japanese auto companies.

Croatian War of Independence: The Battle of the Miljevci Plateau ended after a failed counterattack by forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina against the Croatian Army who had captured the plateau.
Citizens of the United Kingdom voted in favour of leaving the European Union.

links.title: 2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum

facts.text: War of Saint Sabas: In an action off Trapani, Sicily, a Venetian fleet captured all 27 opposing Genoese vessels.
Stand Watie became the last Confederate general of the American Civil War to surrender to Union forces.
The Parliament of Canada passed the Rocky Mountains Park Act, creating Banff National Park in Alberta as the country's first national park.

image.caption: Location in Canada Show map of Canada Banff National Park (Alberta) Show map of Alberta

facts.text: The first instalment of the video-game series Sonic the Hedgehog was released in North America.
Western Roman emperor Glycerius, who was not recognized by his Eastern counterpart Leo I, was forced to abdicate.
In the decisive battle of the First War of Scottish Independence, Scottish forces led by Robert the Bruce defeated English troops under Edward II near Bannockburn, Scotland.
Hundred Years' War: The English fleet commanded by Edward III almost completely destroyed the French fleet at the Battle of Sluys.
The 1559 Book of Common Prayer, a major component of the Elizabethan Religious Settlement, is legally introduced as the liturgy of the Church of England.
Napoleonic Wars: Led by Napoleon, the French Grande Armée crossed the Neman, beginning their invasion of Russia.
" O Canada ", the present-day national anthem of Canada, was first performed in Quebec City during a Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day banquet.
A group of military officers and civilians engineered a bloodless coup in Siam, ending the absolute rule of the Chakri dynasty.
The U.S. Navy's first two fast battleships, North Carolina and Washington, of the North Carolina class, were respectively ordered from the New York and Philadelphia Naval Shipyards.
The first of the Thai cultural mandates was issued, officially changing the country's name from Siam to Thailand.
Second World War: The British Army carried out Operation Collar, its first commando raid into German-occupied France.

links.title: German military administration in occupied France during World War II

facts.text: Following the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre the 13th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party appointed Jiang Zemin as general secretary in place of Zhao Ziyang.

links.title: 13th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party
General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party

facts.text: John Isner defeated Nicolas Mahut at the Wimbledon Championships, concluding the longest match in tennis history, which lasted 11 hours and 5 minutes over three days.

links.title: Isner–Mahut match at the 2010 Wimbledon Championships

facts.text: An outbreak of dancing mania, in which crowds of people danced themselves to exhaustion, began in Aachen (in present-day Germany) before spreading to other parts of Europe.
The first Grand Lodge of Freemasonry, the Premier Grand Lodge of England, was founded in London.
On the Feast of St. John the Baptist, Bach led the first performance of Christ unser Herr zum Jordan kam, BWV 7, the third cantata of his chorale cantata cycle.

links.title: Christ unser Herr zum Jordan kam, BWV 7

facts.text: Amid racial tensions, U.S. Army military police shot and killed a black serviceman after a confrontation at a pub in Bamber Bridge, England.
Julia Gillard was sworn in as the first female prime minister of Australia after incumbent Kevin Rudd declined to contest a leadership spill in the Labor Party.
Second World War: Operation Aerial, an evacuation of nearly 200,000 Allied soldiers from French ports, was completed.
The United Nations Security Council passed Resolution 82 condemning the North Korean invasion of South Korea.
The Korean War began with North Korean forces launching a pre-dawn raid over the 38th parallel into South Korea.
Two cryptographers working for the U.S. National Security Agency left on vacation to Mexico, and proceeded to defect to the Soviet Union.
More than an estimated 400 million people viewed Our World, the first live international satellite television production.

In response to a Freedom of Information Act request, the CIA acknowledged the existence of Area 51, a secretive U.S. Air Force facility in Nevada and a subject of various UFO, and other, conspiracy theories.
Russian invasion of Ukraine: Russian forces captured the city of Sievierodonetsk, Ukraine, after six weeks of fighting.
Anglo-Spanish War: The largest battle ever fought on Jamaica, the three-day Battle of Rio Nuevo, began.
The United States Congress passed the Mann Act, which prohibited the interstate transport of females for "immoral purposes".
World War II: U.S. Navy and Royal Navy ships bombarded Cherbourg, France, to support U.S. Army units engaged in the Battle of Cherbourg.
The rainbow flag representing gay pride was first flown at the San Francisco Gay Freedom Day parade.
Singer Michael Jackson died as a result of the combination of drugs in his body.
Mongol invasions of Anatolia: Mongols achieved a decisive victory over the Seljuq Turks, leading to the decline and disintegration of the Seljuk state.
The Council of Pisa elected Peter of Candia as Alexander V, becoming the third simultaneous claimant of the papacy during the Western Schism.
Julia Gardiner married U.S. President John Tyler at the Church of the Ascension in New York, becoming the first lady.

links.title: First Lady of the United States

facts.text: French authorities suppressed the June Days uprising, in which workers rioted in response to plans to close the National Workshops.
French chemist Henri Moissan successfully isolated elemental fluorine, for which he later won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Bangui, the capital and largest city of the present-day Central African Republic, was founded in French Congo.
The 1906 French Grand Prix, the first Grand Prix motor racing competition, began near Le Mans.
Organized by Vladimir Lenin and Joseph Stalin, among others, Bolshevik revolutionaries robbed a bank stagecoach in Tiflis, present-day Georgia.
World War I: The 26-day Battle of Belleau Wood near the Marne River in France ended with American forces finally clearing that forest of German troops.
J. K. Rowling 's Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone, the first book in the Harry Potter fantasy novel series, is released.

links.title: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone

facts.text: The U.S. Supreme Court struck down sodomy laws in the country in the landmark decision Lawrence v. Texas.

links.title: Supreme Court of the United States
Sodomy laws in the United States
List of landmark court decisions in the United States

facts.text: The U.S. Supreme Court granted federal recognition to same-sex marriage when it overturned the Defense of Marriage Act.

links.title: Supreme Court of the United States
Same-sex marriage in the United States

facts.text: War of Jenkins' Ear: Spanish troops stormed the British-held strategically crucial position of Fort Mose in Spanish Florida.
At a conference in San Francisco, delegates from 50 nations signed a charter establishing the United Nations.

links.title: United Nations Conference on International Organization
Member states of the United Nations

facts.text: A Douglas DC-4 Skymaster aircraft crashed after departing from Perth, becoming the worst peacetime aviation accident in Australia's history.

links.title: 1950 Australian National Airways Douglas DC-4 crash

facts.text: A G20 summit, the largest and most expensive security operation in Canadian history, began in downtown Toronto.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Obergefell v. Hodges that the right of same-sex couples to marry is guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment.

links.title: Supreme Court of the United States
Same-sex marriage in the United States
Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution

facts.text: Queen Elizabeth I issued a royal charter establishing Jesus College, the first Protestant college at the University of Oxford.
War of the Austrian Succession: In the last time that a British monarch led troops in battle, Allied forces commanded by George II (depicted) defeated the French army at Dettingen, Bavaria.
American Civil War: General Sherman 's frontal assault against the Confederate Army of Tennessee failed, but did not stop the Union army from advancing on Atlanta.
One day after surrendering at the Battle of Hakodate, Enomoto Takeaki turned the fort of Goryōkaku over to Japanese forces, signaling the collapse of the Republic of Ezo.
The military phase of the Meiji Restoration in Japan was completed with an imperial victory in the Boshin War.
A. E. J. Collins scored 628 runs not out, the highest recorded score in cricket until being surpassed in 2016.
Jacobo Árbenz resigned as President of Guatemala following a CIA-led coup against his administration.
Hurricane Audrey made landfall near the Texas–Louisiana border, killing over 400 people, mainly in and around Cameron, Louisiana, U.S.
The first identifiable case of Ebola occurred in Sudan.

Croatian War of Independence: As the Yugoslav Army moved into Osijek, Croatia, a civilian attempted to halt them by placing his car in the path of a tank, becoming a symbol of Croatian resistance in the war.
Members of the Japanese cult Aum Shinrikyo released sarin gas in Matsumoto, Nagano, killing eight people and injuring more than five hundred others.
As a result of an ongoing conflict between drug dealers and police in the favelas of Rio de Janeiro, a large military and civil police operation killed 19 people and injured several others.
Robert Mugabe was re-elected as President of Zimbabwe with an overwhelming majority after his opponent Morgan Tsvangirai withdrew, citing violence against his party 's supporters.
Websites of Ukrainian organizations were swamped by a massive cyberattack, blamed on Russian military hackers, using the malware Petya.
The Japanese space probe Hayabusa2 arrived at the asteroid Ryugu to collect samples for return to Earth.
Pope Agatho (depicted), later venerated as a saint in both the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches, began his pontificate.
War of the Second Coalition: French forces won a victory at the Battle of Neuburg, ending Austrian control over the River Danube.
First Russian Revolution: The crew of the Russian battleship Potemkin began a mutiny against their officers.
Korean War: Five North Korean aircraft attacked an American air convoy above Suwon Air Base in the first air engagement of the Korean War.
Ignition of corn starch caused a dust fire at a water park in New Taipei City, Taiwan, killing 15 people and injuring more than 400 others.
Alboin, the king of the Lombards, was assassinated in Verona in a coup d'état instigated by the Byzantines.
Edward IV was crowned King of England at Westminster Abbey.
American Revolutionary War: The militia of the Province of South Carolina repelled a British attack on Charleston.
Giselle, a ballet by the French composer Adolphe Adam, was first performed at the Théâtre de l'Académie Royale de Musique in Paris.

image.caption: Native title Giselle, ou les Wilis

facts.text: Belgian musician Adolphe Sax patented his design of the saxophone.

image.caption: Born Antoine-Joseph Sax ( 1814-11-06 ) 6 November 1814 Dinant (present-day Belgium)

facts.text: The Nakhla meteorite, the first meteorite to suggest signs of aqueous processes on Mars, fell to Earth in Abu Hummus, Egypt.
Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, were assassinated in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip, a Yugoslav nationalist, sparking the outbreak of World War I.

image.caption: Born ( 1894-07-25 ) 25 July 1894 Obljaj , Condominium of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Austria-Hungary

facts.text: First World War: Around 55,000 workers in Berlin went on strike to protest against the trial of anti-war campaigner Karl Liebknecht.
World War II: The Wehrmacht launched Case Blue, a strategic German offensive to capture oil fields in the south of the Soviet Union.
Polish workers demanding better working conditions began massive protests in Poznań, but were later violently repressed by the Polish People's Army and the Internal Security Corps.
Profumo affair: During the trial of Stephen Ward, Mandy Rice-Davies uttered the phrase " Well he would, wouldn't he? "
In response to a police raid at the Stonewall Inn in New York City, groups of gay and transgender people began demonstrations, a watershed event for the worldwide gay rights movement.

In Regents of the University of California v. Bakke, the U.S. Supreme Court barred quota systems in college admissions but held that affirmative-action programs advantaging minorities were constitutional.

links.title: Regents of the University of California v. Bakke
Supreme Court of the United States

facts.text: President Slobodan Milošević gave a speech at Gazimestan in which he described the possibility of "armed battles" in the future of Serbia's national development.
Paperback Software, a company founded by Adam Osborne, was found guilty of copyright infringement for using Lotus 1-2-3 's look-and-feel interface in its own spreadsheet program.
Gunmen attacked Istanbul's Atatürk Airport, killing 45 people and injuring more than 230 others.
Police captured Australian bank robber and cultural icon Ned Kelly after a gun battle in Glenrowan, Victoria.

image.caption: Born Edward Kelly ( 1854-12-00 ) December 1854 [ a ] Beveridge , Colony of Victoria , Australia

facts.text: The U.S. Court of Private Land Claims ruled that James Reavis 's claim to 18,600 sq mi (48,000 km 2 ) of land in present-day Arizona and New Mexico was "wholly fictitious and fraudulent".

links.title: United States Court of Private Land Claims

facts.text: In the worst maritime disaster involving a Danish merchant ship, SS Norge ran aground on Hasselwood Rock and sank in the North Atlantic, resulting in more than 635 deaths.
Korean War: South Korean forces began the Bodo League massacre, summarily executing tens of thousands of suspected North Korean sympathizers.
The first privateer battle of the American Revolutionary War, the Battle of Turtle Gut Inlet, was fought near Cape May, New Jersey.
Black Hawk War: Three men working in a cornfield were attacked by Sauk Native Americans, resulting in two deaths.

A passenger train fell through an open swing bridge into the Richelieu River near present-day Mont-Saint-Hilaire, Quebec, killing as many as 99 people and injuring 100 others in Canada's worst railway accident.
Hyde Park and several other Illinois townships voted to be annexed by Chicago, forming the largest city by area in the United States and the second-largest by population.
More than 50,000 Union and Confederate veterans gathered at the Gettysburg Battlefield, the largest combined reunion of American Civil War veterans ever held.
The United States Army Air Corps aircraft Bird of Paradise landed at Wheeler Field on the Hawaiian island of Oahu to complete the first transpacific flight.

The Soyuz 11 spacecraft experienced uncontrolled decompression during preparations for reentry, killing Soviet cosmonauts Vladislav Volkov, Georgy Dobrovolsky and Viktor Patsayev —the only human deaths to have occurred in space.
Atlantis became the first U.S. Space Shuttle to dock with the Russian space station Mir as part of the Shuttle– Mir program.
An overloaded balcony collapsed in Chicago, United States, killing 13 people and injuring 57 others.
The original Globe Theatre in London burned to the ground after a cannon employed for special effects misfired during a performance of Henry VIII and ignited the roof.
One of the strongest tornadoes in history struck Woldegk in present-day northeastern Germany, killing one person.
The United States defeated England during the FIFA World Cup in one of the greatest upsets in the competition's history.

links.title: United States men's national soccer team
United States v England (1950 FIFA World Cup)

facts.text: Actress Jayne Mansfield, her boyfriend Sam Brody, and their driver were killed in a car accident outside of New Orleans, while her children Miklós, Zoltán, and Mariska Hargitay escaped with only minor injuries.

image.caption: Born Vera Jayne Palmer ( 1933-04-19 ) April 19, 1933 Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania , U.S.

facts.text: Reddit banned r/The_Donald, a pro-Trump subreddit, for rule violations and antagonizing the company.
Zhu Yunwen ascended the throne to the Ming dynasty to become the Jianwen Emperor.
During a jousting match, King Henry II of France was mortally wounded when fragments of Gabriel Montgomery 's lance pierced his eye.

links.title: Gabriel de Lorges, Count of Montgomery

facts.text: French acrobat Charles Blondin crossed Niagara Gorge, making him one of the world's most famous tightrope walkers.
Tower Bridge, a combined bascule and suspension bridge over the River Thames in London, was inaugurated.
German chancellor Adolf Hitler began a purge of the paramilitary wing of the Nazi Party and other political rivals, executing at least 85 people.

links.title: Victims of the Night of the Long Knives

facts.text: The National Organization for Women, a leading United States feminist organization, was founded in Washington, D.C.
Municipal workers in Baltimore, Maryland, went on strike seeking higher wages and better conditions.
Ryan White, an HIV/AIDS patient in the U.S., was denied re-admission to his school after he had contracted the disease from hemophilia treatments.
A building fire in Atlanta killed five people.
Yemenia Flight 626 crashed into the Indian Ocean near the Comoros, killing 152 people, with French schoolgirl Bahia Bakari the sole survivor.

links.title: List of sole survivors of aviation accidents and incidents

facts.text: Anglo-Spanish War: After a 15-day siege Spanish troops in San Juan, modern-day Puerto Rico, surrendered to an English force under Sir George Clifford.
Nadir of American race relations: A mob of white Americans killed eight people in Oconee County, Georgia, as part of a mass lynching.
The Belgian Congo gained independence from colonial rule, beginning a period of instability that would lead to the dictatorship of Joseph-Désiré Mobutu.
The coronation of Pope Paul VI took place, the last such ceremony before its abandonment by later popes.
An Indonesian Air Force military transport aircraft crashed near a residential neighborhood in Medan, killing 139 people.

links.title: 2015 Sumatra Indonesian Air Force C-130 crash
